title: The work integral has an observable endpoint
question: What energy is required to accelerate an electron?
recap: Integrating the longitudinal force gives kinetic energy mc²(γ − 1), not the total rest energy. Accelerating voltage and curvature provide separate experimental relations under specified fields.
premises: Use invariant mass m, subluminal speed, and the stated force convention.
For the voltage relation, the particle begins at rest and field work becomes kinetic energy.
limitations: The ideal treatment excludes radiation loss and material interactions.
A kinetic-energy expression alone does not derive the September statement about changing rest energy.

overview.text: Integrating the longitudinal force gives kinetic energy mc²(γ − 1), not the total rest energy. Accelerating voltage and curvature provide separate experimental relations under specified fields.

full.spoken: Integrating the longitudinal work from rest gives m c squared times gamma minus one.

full.text: Use dγ/du = γ³u/c² to evaluate the integral. Near zero speed, K approaches mv²/2. At 0.6c the exact value is 0.25mc² whereas the quadratic approximation is 0.18mc², so the approximation error is visible.

full.spoken: For acceleration from rest, charge magnitude times voltage magnitude supplies kinetic energy; in a transverse magnetic field the circular radius is gamma m v over charge magnitude B.

full.text: The third relation compares electric and magnetic deflection, with force and acceleration conventions kept explicit. In a purely transverse electric field the instantaneous curvature radius is γmv²/(|q|E). The electron-dynamics laboratory separates that local curvature from a magnetic circular orbit at constant speed.

full.returnCaption: Return to what energy is required to accelerate an electron.

items: Write longitudinal force as mγ³ times acceleration.
Multiply by displacement, using a dx = u du.
Integrate from rest and use the derivative of gamma.
Compare the exact value with the low-speed expansion without calling them equal at 0.6c.
For a voltage estimate, use charge magnitude and state the energy-loss assumption.
For deflection, distinguish magnetic constant-speed curvature from an instantaneous transverse electric curvature.

margin.text: The three experimental relations do not erase model assumptions about fields and radiation loss. The acknowledgment to M. Besso and the June 1905 closing belong to the source edition; this preview does not claim to transcribe or align those blocks.
